newsitem.title: USA: Clinton administration unveils IRS reform plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton administration unveils IRS reform plan.

text.p: The Clinton administration Monday unveiled a plan to reform the troubled Internal Revenue Service, long a symbol of a tax system that many feel is unfair and everyone agrees is needlessly complex.
The IRS has been under heavy fire from Congress for mismanaged and failed attempts at updating technology and for insensitive treatment of taxpayers.
Critics charge that despite some $4 billion in spending over the past decade, there has been little if any improvement in processing tax returns or in computer and phone answering systems.

The new plan, outlined in a speech by Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers to the Tax Executives Institute, focuses on improving IRS management and seeks a new commissioner skilled in customer service, organisational change and information technolgy.
At a new briefing, Summers said he hoped the reform effort would not become embroiled in political wrangling about the tax-collecting agency and its place in government.

"This is an issue that really shouldn't be about politics -- answering the phone better, not billing peple who shouldn't be billed, collecting all the taxes that are owed," Summers said, adding there was room for a bipartisan effort.
The Clinton administration's reform proposal comes less than a month before Americans go through the annual ordeal of paying their taxes before the April 15 deadline.
The ultimate measure of its success will be how taxpayers come to perceive the IRS, Summers said.

"If the IRS earns not necessarily the affection but the respect of the American people for the way they do their job, we will have succeeded," he said. He emphasised there will be "benchmarks" for measuring the IRS' progress in such areas as answering phones and cutting down on incorrect billing.
Summers made clear that making the IRS work better should not be confused with various plans to update or even scrap the nation's tax system and the IRS along with it.
"The IRS needs to be more responsive to taxpayers, to use technology more effectively and to be more efficient," Summers told the tax executives.
He said he believed the United States would have an income tax based on the ability of people to pay for the foreseeable future and the IRS would be needed to administer it.

Control and oversight of the IRS should be kept within the administration, rather than farmed out to an independent board, Summers said, likening it to the existing system of active civil management over the armed forces.
"Experience suggests that a direct executive responsibility really is most potent in bringing about change," he added.
In response to questions, he said he did not believe there should be a conflict with Congress about reforming the IRS.

"I think it should be understood by all that decisions about customer service strategy, about whether and how best to pursue electronic filing, the overall effort devoted to enforcement....have nothing to do with individual taxpayers," Summers said.

"We are barred by law from involvement in cases involving specific taxpayers, except in the most carefully delineated exceptions, which we have not availed ourselves of and we expect to continue to live within those strictures," he added.
Control over the IRS is a sensitive issue for fear its investigative powers could be turned on political opponents.
Summers said the complexity of the tax code and problems at the IRS should not be used to sell extreme measures such as the much-discussed flat tax that he said are complex and unfair in themselves.
"What we must not do is attack the IRS in order to promote other agendas," Summers said.
Summers said reforms would give the IRS more flexibility, allowing it to enhance and strengthen its operations without having its hands tied by bureaucratic red tape.
"The IRS faces a multitude of restrictions -- restrictions that would be unacceptable in the private sector -- that hamper its ability to provide efficient service," Summers said.
In addition, Summers said the administration would work with Congress to help the IRS get the stable and predictable funding it needs to operate more effectively.
"Today, the IRS operates in a low-trust, short-tether budgeting environment," he told the meeting. "This makes rational planning for capital projects such as information technology very difficult."
But Summers also made clear that the administration was committed to simplifying the tax code, noting that the president has proposed to exclude up to $500,000 of capital gains on the sale of a home.
This will "dramtically simplify record keeping for more than 60 million families," he said.
